ISO 7708 — Air quality — Particle size fraction definitions

scope: All portable and wheeled fire extinguishers at the mine site, including those in buildings, mobile equipment, workshops, magazines, offices, and outdoor locations.
objective: Ensure all fire extinguishers are maintained in serviceable condition and ready for immediate use through regular inspection, maintenance, and hydrostatic testing.
responsibilities: Fire Warden: conducts monthly visual inspections of fire extinguishers in assigned areas, reports deficiencies, ensures extinguishers are accessible.
Maintenance Technician: conducts annual maintenance inspection (discharge/recharge or internal examination), hydrostatic testing, and documentation.
HSE Officer: manages fire extinguisher inventory, ensures compliance with inspection schedule, conducts training on extinguisher use, arranges external servicing.
All Personnel: know location and use of nearest fire extinguisher, do not tamper with or obstruct extinguishers, report missing or damaged extinguishers immediately.
procedure_steps: 1. Monthly Visual Inspection (by Fire Warden): Verify extinguisher is in designated location, not moved or obstructed. Check pressure gauge — needle must be in the green (operable) zone. Inspect for physical damage: dents, corrosion, leaking, cracked hose. Verify safety pin and tamper seal are intact. Check instruction label is legible and facing outward. Record inspection on monthly inspection tag — sign and date.

2. Annual Maintenance Inspection (by Maintenance Technician): Remove extinguisher from service. Perform external examination: check for corrosion, damage, legible labels, condition of hose and nozzle. Check operating mechanism — lever, handle, valve assembly. Weigh or measure agent charge — must be within ±10% of marked weight (for stored-pressure types). For stored-pressure: check pressure gauge reading. Verify emergency discharge and recharge capability. Record all findings on maintenance tag and in fire extinguisher register.

3. Hydrostatic Testing: Schedule hydrostatic test per NFPA 10 requirements: Class ABC dry chemical: every 12 years. Class CO₂: every 12 years. Class K (wet chemical): every 5 years. Class D (special): per manufacturer recommendation. Extinguishers that fail hydrostatic test must be destroyed — do not attempt repair. Use only licensed hydrostatic testing facility.

4. Recharging: Recharge extinguishers immediately after any use (even partial). Use only manufacturer-approved agents — never substitute. Recharging must be performed by trained technician with proper equipment. After recharge: weigh, pressurize (stored-pressure types), and update maintenance record. Place back in service within 24 hours.

5. Placement Requirements: Maximum travel distance: 23 meters (75 feet) for Class A hazards, 15 meters (50 feet) for Class B hazards. Mount extinguishers: handle height 0.9-1.5 meters above floor. Wheeled extinguishers: located at strategic points near high-hazard areas. Visibility: clear line of sight or appropriate signage. Access: do not lock in rooms without emergency access provisions.

6. Extinguisher Types by Hazard Area: Class A (water, foam): offices, workshops, general areas. Class B (CO₂, dry chemical, foam): fuel storage, flammable liquid areas, vehicle workshops. Class C (dry chemical, CO₂): electrical rooms, motor control centers. Class D (dry powder): metalworking areas, titanium/magnesium machining. Class K (wet chemical): kitchens, dining facilities. ABC (multipurpose dry chemical): general use throughout site.

7. Training: All personnel: annual fire extinguisher use training (P.A.S.S. — Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep). Fire wardens: additional training on fire extinguisher types, inspection procedures, and fire response. Training documented with date, trainer, and attendees. Refresher training: when extinguisher types change or new hazards identified.

8. Recordkeeping: Maintain fire extinguisher register: location, type, size, serial number, manufacture date, last inspection, last maintenance, next hydrostatic test date. Monthly inspection tags: signed and dated. Annual maintenance records: filed with fire safety documentation. Hydrostatic test certificates: retained for life of extinguisher.

emergency_response: If fire extinguisher fails during use: evacuate area, activate fire alarm, use alternative extinguisher or hose. If extinguisher damage or leakage found during inspection: remove from service immediately, replace with spare. If extinguisher accidentally discharged: evacuate area, ventilate, recharge or replace. Report any fire extinguisher failure to HSE Manager.

scope: All personnel at the mine site, including surface and underground operations, processing plant, workshops, offices, and remote field locations. Applies to all medical emergencies from minor injuries to life-threatening conditions.
objective: Provide immediate, effective first aid to injured or ill persons at the mine site to preserve life, prevent deterioration, and promote recovery until professional medical care is available.
responsibilities: First Aider (trained): provides immediate first aid at the scene, activates emergency response, communicates patient condition to incoming EMS.
Shift Supervisor: activates site emergency response, secures the scene, ensures first aid kit availability, coordinates ambulance dispatch.
HSE Manager: manages first aid training program, maintains first aid equipment inventory, reviews all first aid incidents, ensures compliance with regulatory first aid requirements.
Site Medical Officer (if available): provides advanced first aid, medical triage, coordinates patient evacuation to hospital, manages medical records.
procedure_steps: 1. Scene Assessment and Safety: Assess scene for ongoing hazards — do not become a second victim. Make scene safe before approaching patient (de-energize equipment, control traffic, extinguish fire). Wear appropriate PPE — gloves minimum, face shield for blood/body fluid exposure risk. Activate site emergency response if scene requires additional resources.

2. Primary Survey (DRABC): Danger — check for dangers to rescuer and patient. Response — check patient responsiveness (shout and gently shake). Airway — open airway using head tilt-chin lift (jaw thrust if spinal injury suspected). Breathing — look, listen, feel for breathing for 10 seconds. Circulation — check for severe bleeding, skin color, temperature.

3. Cardiac Arrest / CPR: If unresponsive and not breathing normally: begin CPR immediately. Compression-to-ventilation ratio: 30:2 (trained rescuer) or compression-only (untrained). Compression rate: 100-120 per minute. Compression depth: 5-6 cm for adults. Use AED as soon as available — follow device prompts. Continue CPR until patient recovers, EMS arrives, or rescuer is physically unable to continue.

4. Severe Bleeding Control: Apply direct pressure with sterile dressing or clean cloth. If bleeding not controlled: apply tourniquet 5-7 cm above wound (for limb injuries only). Elevate injured limb above heart level if possible. Apply pressure dressing if direct pressure insufficient. For impaled objects: do not remove — stabilize in place with bulky dressing.

5. Burns First Aid: Thermal burns: cool with cool (not ice cold) running water for 20 minutes. Remove clothing and jewelry from burned area — do not remove adhered clothing. Cover with sterile, non-adherent dressing. Do not apply creams, oils, or home remedies. Chemical burns: flush with copious water for minimum 20 minutes. Remove contaminated clothing. Electrical burns: ensure power source is off before touching patient. Check for entry and exit wounds.

6. Fractures and Musculoskeletal Injuries: Immobilize suspected fractures using splints — padded, immobilize joint above and below fracture. Check distal circulation, sensation, and movement (CSM) before and after splinting. For suspected spinal injury: do not move patient — maintain manual in-line stabilization. Apply ice wrapped in cloth to reduce swelling (20 minutes on, 20 minutes off).

7. Eye Injuries: Chemical splash: flush eye with clean water or saline for minimum 15 minutes — hold eyelids open. Seek immediate medical attention. Foreign body: do not rub eye. Irrigate with water. If foreign body cannot be flushed, cover eye with eye shield and seek medical attention. Impact injury: do not apply pressure. Cover eye with sterile shield and seek medical attention.

8. Emergency Communication: Activate site emergency response by radio or phone. Provide: location (GPS coordinates or specific location description), nature of injury/illness, number of patients, current patient condition, assistance needed. Assign someone to meet ambulance and guide to patient location.

scope: All spill response activities at the mine site for spills of fuels, lubricants, chemicals, process solutions, cyanide solutions, acids, and any substance that could contaminate soil, surface water, or groundwater.
objective: Provide a rapid, effective response to spills and releases of hazardous substances to minimize environmental damage, worker exposure, and regulatory non-compliance.
responsibilities: First Responder (initial): discovers or responds to spill, contains spill at source if safe to do so, activates spill response alarm, initiates initial containment.
Spill Response Team: trained HAZMAT responders, deploys spill containment and cleanup equipment, manages spill remediation, oversees waste disposal.
Environmental Officer: assesses environmental impact, reports spills to regulatory authority as required, manages site remediation, maintains spill records.
Site Manager: authorizes major spill response expenditures, communicates with regulators and community, oversees incident investigation.
procedure_steps: 1. Immediate Response (First Responder): Assess spill: identify substance, approximate quantity, direction of flow, potential for waterway contact. Alert area personnel — sound alarm if spill is >5 liters or involves hazardous material. If safe: stop the source (close valve, plug leak, right overturned container). Contain: deploy spill berms, absorbent booms, or soil around spill perimeter to prevent spread. Do NOT attempt to contain spills involving unknown, highly toxic, or corrosive materials — evacuate area.

2. Notification and Activation: Notify Shift Supervisor and Spill Response Team immediately. For spills >100 liters or spills reaching waterways: activate site emergency response and notify Environmental Officer. For reportable spills: contact regulatory authority within required timeframe (typically 1-24 hours depending on jurisdiction and severity). Activate upstream/downstream water monitoring.

3. Spill Classification: Minor spill: <10 liters, contained on site, no waterway contact. Handled by first responder with spill kit. Medium spill: 10-200 liters, contained on site, no waterway contact. Spill Response Team deploys. Major spill: >200 liters, or any spill reaching waterway, or involving cyanide/critical chemical. Full emergency response, regulatory notification, potential site evacuation.

4. Containment and Recovery: Absorbent application: apply absorbent granules or pads to spill — work from outside perimeter inward. Skimming: for floating oils/fuels on water — deploy skimmers and absorbent booms. Pumping: for large liquid spills — use portable pumps to transfer to temporary storage tanks. Soil removal: excavate contaminated soil — remove to depth of contamination confirmed by field testing.

5. Waterway Protection: If spill may reach waterway: deploy absorbent booms across watercourse. Activate diversion berms to redirect clean water around spill. Install containment at waterway entry points. Sample water upstream and downstream of spill. Notify downstream water users if waterway is affected.

6. Decontamination: Personnel decontamination: wash with appropriate solvent or detergent depending on substance. Equipment decontamination: clean and survey before returning to service. Vehicle decontamination: wash down before leaving contaminated area. Area decontamination: remove all visible contamination, then sample to confirm clean.

7. Waste Disposal: Collect contaminated absorbent, soil, and materials in labeled hazardous waste containers. Characterize waste per regulatory requirements ( TCLP testing for metals, pH, ignitability). Dispose of through licensed hazardous waste contractor. Maintain waste manifests and disposal records. For cyanide spills: treat with cyanide destruction before disposal.

8. Post-Spill Actions: Document spill: date, time, location, substance, quantity, cause, response actions, environmental impact. Conduct root cause analysis for spills >50 liters or all cyanide spills. Implement corrective actions to prevent recurrence. Update spill response plan if deficiencies identified. Report final spill report to regulatory authority per requirements. Conduct post-incident debrief with spill response team.

Chemical-resistant gloves (nitrile or neoprene — consult SDS)
Safety goggles (under respirator facepiece or standalone for minor spills)
hazards: Acute chemical exposure from spill contents
Environmental contamination of surface water and groundwater
Fire or explosion from flammable liquid spills
Slip hazards from spilled liquids on roadways and working surfaces

emergency_response: Activate site emergency response for major spills. Evacuate upwind and uphill from spill. For personnel exposure: remove contaminated clothing, flush affected skin with water for 15 minutes, seek medical attention. For cyanide spill: follow Cyanide Handling SOP emergency procedures. For flammable liquid spill: eliminate ignition sources, evacuate area, deploy foam if fire risk is high. Contact environmental regulatory authority for reportable spills.
